items.readable_text:
Content:
Finding the cube root of a number is the reverse of cubing a number. We express the cube root using the radical symbol [MATH: \sqrt[3]{\phantom{x}}.]

Content:
For example, the "cube root of [MATH: 8]" equals [MATH: \color{blue}2] since

Content:
[MATH: {\color{blue}2}^3 = {\color{blue}2}\cdot {\color{blue}2}\cdot {\color{blue}2} = 8.]

Content:
So, we write [MATH: \sqrt[3]{8}={\color{blue}2}.]

Content:
Some basic cube roots are as follows:

Content:
[MATH: root(0, 3)|=|root(0^{3}, 3)|=|0; root(1, 3)|=|root(1^{3}, 3)|=|1; root(8, 3)|=|root(2^{3}, 3)|=|2; root(27, 3)|=|root(3^{3}, 3)|=|3; root(64, 3)|=|root(4^{3}, 3)|=|4; root(125, 3)|=|root(5^{3}, 3)|=|5; root(1000, 3)|=|root(10^{3}, 3)|=|10]

Content:
A perfect cube is a number whose cube root is a whole number. So, the numbers

Content:
[MATH: 0,\qquad 1,\qquad 8,\qquad 27,\qquad 64,\qquad 125, \qquad 1\,000]
are all perfect cubes. You need to remember them.

items.title: Finding the Cube Root of a Positive Perfect Cube

sections.normalized_html:
First, notice that the numbers [MATH: 1] and [MATH: 64] are both perfect cubes.

So, to determine the value of [MATH: \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{1}{64}},] we express [MATH: \dfrac{1}{64}] as a perfect cube:

[MATH: root((1)/(64), 3)|=; root((1^{3})/(4^{3}), 3)|=; root((1 ⋅ 1 ⋅ 1)/(4 ⋅ 4 ⋅ 4), 3)|=; root((1)/(4) ⋅ (1)/(4) ⋅ (1)/(4), 3)|=; root(((1)/(4))^{3}, 3)|=; (1)/(4)]

items.title: The Cube Root of a Negative Perfect Cube

sections.normalized_html: Unlike the square root, it is possible to find the cube root of a negative number.
sections.readable_text: Unlike the square root, it is possible to find the cube root of a negative number.

items.readable_text:
Content:
Unlike the square root, it is possible to find the cube root of a negative number.

Content:
For example, [MATH: \sqrt[3]{-8}={\color{blue}{-2}}] because

Content:
[MATH: -8 = ({\color{blue}{-2}})^3 = ({\color{blue}{-2}})\cdot ({\color{blue}{-2}})\cdot ({\color{blue}{-2}}).]

Content:
Some basic cube roots of negative numbers are as follows:
[MATH: root(− 1, 3)|=|root((− 1)^{3}, 3)|=|− 1; root(− 8, 3)|=|root((− 2)^{3}, 3)|=|− 2; root(− 27, 3)|=|root((− 3)^{3}, 3)|=|− 3; root(− 64, 3)|=|root((− 4)^{3}, 3)|=|− 4; root(− 125, 3)|=|root((− 5)^{3}, 3)|=|− 5; root(− 1000, 3)|=|root((− 10)^{3}, 3)|=|− 10]

Content:
Note that the numbers

Content:
[MATH: -1,\qquad -8,\qquad -27,\qquad -64,\qquad -125, \qquad -1\,000]

Content:
are all perfect cubes.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Finding the cube root of a number is the reverse of cubing a number. We express the cube root using the radical symbol [MATH: \sqrt[3]{\phantom{x}}.]

Content:
For example, the "cube root of [MATH: 8]" equals [MATH: \color{blue}2] since

Content:
[MATH: {\color{blue}2}^3 = {\color{blue}2}\cdot {\color{blue}2}\cdot {\color{blue}2} = 8.]

Content:
So, we write [MATH: \sqrt[3]{8}={\color{blue}2}.]

Content:
Some basic cube roots are as follows:

Content:
[MATH: root(0, 3)|=|root(0^{3}, 3)|=|0; root(1, 3)|=|root(1^{3}, 3)|=|1; root(8, 3)|=|root(2^{3}, 3)|=|2; root(27, 3)|=|root(3^{3}, 3)|=|3; root(64, 3)|=|root(4^{3}, 3)|=|4; root(125, 3)|=|root(5^{3}, 3)|=|5; root(1000, 3)|=|root(10^{3}, 3)|=|10]

Content:
A perfect cube is a number whose cube root is a whole number. So, the numbers

Content:
[MATH: 0,\qquad 1,\qquad 8,\qquad 27,\qquad 64,\qquad 125, \qquad 1\,000]
are all perfect cubes. You need to remember them.

---

Item 10 — Tutorial: The Cube Root of a Negative Perfect Cube

Content:
Unlike the square root, it is possible to find the cube root of a negative number.

Content:
For example, [MATH: \sqrt[3]{-8}={\color{blue}{-2}}] because

Content:

Content:

Content:
Note that the numbers

Content:
[MATH: -1,\qquad -8,\qquad -27,\qquad -64,\qquad -125, \qquad -1\,000]

are all perfect cubes.

Item 15 — Tutorial: Cubing a Cube Root

Content:
Let's calculate [MATH: (\sqrt[3]{64})^3] by performing each operation one step at a time:
[MATH: \left(\sqrt[3]{\color{blue}64}\right)^3 = \left(\sqrt[3]{{\color{red}4}^3}\right)^3 = {\color{red}4}^3 = {\color{blue}64}]
Notice that cubing the cube root gives the number under the cube root:
[MATH: \left( \sqrt[3]{64} \right)^3 = 64]

Content:
This result holds in general. If [MATH: \color{blue}\square] is any number, then
[MATH: \left(\sqrt[3]{\color{blue}\square}\right)^3 = {\color{blue}\square}.]

Content:
The cube and the cube root cancel each other out, and we're left with the number that we started with.
